transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I came in because my head just feels… foggy, I suppose is the best word for it. I keep mixing up things that really ought to be simple. Like appointment times—I’ll be sure something is at one time and then realize I had it wrong. And I’ve been getting confused about exhibit dates, which is embarrassing because I try to keep those things straight. I also find myself wondering which volunteer I already called, and then I’m afraid I’m either bothering someone twice or forgetting someone completely.

It’s not that I don’t care or I’m not trying. I write things down, but somehow it still feels like the information gets all tangled in my head. That’s what made me think I’d better come talk to someone.
Are these memory and confusion issues happening in all parts of your life, or do they seem to be limited mostly to things like appointments and volunteer work?

It’s mostly the kinds of things I mentioned, I think—appointments, the dates for exhibits, and keeping straight who I’ve called for volunteering. Those are the ones that stand out because they’re simple things I used to manage without so much effort, and now I’ll be sure I have it right and then find out I don’t.

I wouldn’t say I’ve made a careful list of every part of my life, but what brought me in was that foggy feeling, like the information just gets jumbled. It’s especially noticeable when I’m trying to keep track of schedules or little responsibilities, and then I start second-guessing myself—did I write that down right, did I already call her, was that exhibit this week or next week. That’s the sort of confusion that’s been bothering me.
Have you noticed any confusion or difficulties when dealing with more complex tasks or unfamiliar situations, or is it mainly with simple, routine things like appointments and schedules?

It seems mainly with the simple, routine things, which is what’s so frustrating. I mean, I’m not talking about doing some complicated new project or figuring out something I’ve never seen before. What made me come in is more that my head feels foggy with things that ought to be ordinary—appointment times, the dates for exhibits, and remembering which volunteer I already called.

I’ll think, “All right, I’ve got that straight,” and then later I realize I mixed it up, or I’m suddenly unsure and have to check again. And then even after checking, I can get myself turned around. It’s like the information doesn’t sit in the right place in my head anymore. The little everyday details get tangled, and that’s what’s been worrying me.
Do you find yourself getting confused more easily in places you know well, like your home or neighborhood, or does it tend to happen more in new or unfamiliar settings?

I don’t think it’s so much about the place, really. I haven’t noticed myself getting confused because I’m in my own neighborhood or because I’m somewhere new, exactly. What stands out more is that my head feels foggy no matter where I am, and then I mix up these simple things that I should be able to keep straight.

Like an appointment time—I’ll be sure it’s one time, and then I’ll look again and realize I had it wrong, or I’ll get myself all turned around about it. Or with the exhibit dates, I’ll think I know which week something is happening, and then suddenly I’m not sure at all. And the volunteer calls are another one, because I’ll sit there thinking, “Did I already call her, or was that someone else?” It’s those little details that seem to get tangled up in my head. So I wouldn’t say it’s home versus unfamiliar places so much as just… ordinary information not staying clear.
Do you ever find yourself getting confused about what day it is or what time of year it is, like not knowing if it’s the current month or not remembering what season it is?

I don’t think so… not in that way, at least. I mean, I can usually tell you what day it is if I stop and think, and I know what month or season we’re in. I’m not waking up thinking it’s spring when it’s fall or anything like that.

What happens is more like I’ll lose track of a date on the calendar, or I’ll think an appointment is on Tuesday and then it turns out it was Wednesday, or I’ll get the week of something mixed up. So it’s not that I don’t know what time of year it is. It’s more the exact day or the scheduling details that get slippery, if that makes sense. I may have to look at the calendar more than once, and then I get annoyed with myself because I feel like I should have remembered it.
Do you ever have trouble recognizing people you know well, like close family members or friends, or do you sometimes forget your own name or personal details?

No, I don’t think I’ve had anything like that. I recognize my family and my friends, the people I know well. I might take a second sometimes if I see someone out of context, you know, like if I run into somebody at the store when I usually only see them at church or at an event, but then I know who they are. It’s not that I’m looking at my daughter or a close friend and not knowing them.

And I haven’t forgotten my own name or things like that. I know who I am. I know my personal details. That’s not really the problem. The things that bother me are more the smaller bits of information that I’m supposed to keep organized, not recognizing people or forgetting myself.
Do you ever find that the confusion gets bad enough that you have trouble handling everyday tasks on your own, like managing your finances, preparing meals, or taking your medications as scheduled?

Yes… I mean, I hate to say it that way, because I don’t like feeling like I can’t manage my own life, but it has started to affect things I used to handle just fine.

I’ve missed doctor visits because I had the time or the day wrong, or I thought I had written it down and then couldn’t find where. And the senior center schedule—oh, that got all tangled up. I used to be able to keep track of who was calling whom, what event was on which day, what needed to be arranged, and lately it’s like I get one piece of it wrong and then the whole thing is off. I’ll make a call and then not remember if I actually did it, or I’ll have the calendar in front of me and still somehow get confused.

My husband has had to step in more than I want to admit. He helps with the calls now, and with the calendars, and even with repair decisions around the house that I used to just take care of myself. It’s embarrassing, honestly. I can still do things, but I don’t trust myself the same way, so I’ll ask him to double-check or he’ll just quietly take over when he sees I’m getting turned around.
Do you ever feel uncertain about the current day, like you're not quite sure if it's today, tomorrow, or another day, even beyond just forgetting scheduled events?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way, no. I don’t usually feel like I don’t know whether it’s today or tomorrow, exactly. I might wake up and have to think for a minute, like, “All right, what day is this?” especially if there isn’t something obvious on the schedule, but once I look at the calendar or think through what happened yesterday, I can place myself.

It’s more that the days kind of run together sometimes, and then I get anxious that I’ve missed something or mixed something up. But I don’t think I’m sitting there truly believing it’s another day, if that makes sense. It’s more uncertainty around keeping it straight than not knowing what day I’m in.
Do you ever find yourself unsure about the current date, month, or year, even after checking a calendar or being reminded?

No, I don’t think so… not like that. I mean, I can get mixed up with the date sometimes if I haven’t looked at the calendar yet, or I might say, “Is it the 12th or the 13th?”—that kind of thing. But once I check the calendar or someone tells me, it usually settles in.

I don’t think I’ve been unsure of the month or the year after being reminded. If I look at it, I can say, “Okay, yes, that’s right.” It’s more that I don’t always keep it right at the front of my mind, especially when the days feel the same, but I’m not sitting there staring at the calendar and still not understanding what month or year it is. At least I haven’t noticed that happening.
Have you ever found yourself repeatedly confused about the current date, month, or year, even after being reminded or checking a calendar?

No, not repeatedly like that, I don’t think so. I mean, I do get turned around sometimes with the exact date, especially if the week has been quiet and one day feels like the next, but if I check the calendar or my husband says, “It’s Tuesday, the 14th,” then I usually go, “Oh, right, okay,” and I can hold onto it.

I wouldn’t say I’m looking at the calendar over and over and still not knowing what month it is or what year it is. That would frighten me, honestly, and I don’t think that’s been happening. It’s more the ordinary sort of mix-up with the number of the day, or needing to double-check, rather than being truly confused after I’ve been reminded.
Do you ever find it difficult to follow a sequence of steps, like following a recipe, putting something together, or managing something that requires several steps in order?

Yes… yes, I do think that’s part of what’s been bothering me. I don’t know if I’d say I can’t follow steps at all, but my head feels foggy, and I keep mixing up simple things that I really should be able to keep straight.

Like with appointments, I’ll write something down and then later I’m not sure if I’ve got the time right, or I’ll think an appointment is at one time and then realize I had it wrong. And with exhibit dates—things I used to keep organized more easily—I’ll get the dates muddled in my head and have to go back and check again. It’s embarrassing, because these aren’t complicated things, you know? They’re the sort of ordinary details I used to manage.

And even with calling volunteers, I’ll start to lose track of who I already called and who I only meant to call. Then I’m sitting there with my notes trying to piece it together, and it makes me feel like I can’t quite trust my own thinking. That fogginess, and the mixing things up, is really what brought me in.
Do you ever lose track of the sequence of days or dates, like not being able to tell if something happened yesterday or a few days ago, even after thinking about it?

Yes, I think I do, at least in the sense that things don’t line up in my head the way they should. I can usually figure it out if I really sit down and look at my notes or the calendar, but it takes more effort than it used to, and I’ll get this foggy feeling like I’m trying to sort through papers in my mind.

It’s less like I don’t know what day it is at all, and more like I’ll mix up when something happened or when something is supposed to happen. I’ll think an appointment was one time, then look again and realize I had it wrong. Or with the exhibit dates, I’ll have this whole idea in my head of what comes first and what comes after, and then I second-guess it and have to check again. Same with calling volunteers—I’ll think, “Did I call her yesterday? Or did I only mean to call her?” and then I’m going back through my notes trying to piece it together.

That’s really the part that worries me. These are simple things, ordinary things, and my head just feels foggy and I keep mixing them up.
Even after being reminded or checking a calendar, do you still find it hard to keep track of the day, date, or the order of days?

Yes, though maybe not in the sense that I don’t know what year it is or anything like that. It’s more… once I’ve checked, I can usually say, “All right, today is Wednesday,” or whatever it is, but keeping the order of things straight in my head is where I get muddled.

What really brought me in is this foggy feeling, like my thinking just isn’t as clear as it used to be. I’ll check an appointment time and then later I’m uncertain again, like, “Was it 10:30 or 1:30?” And with the exhibit dates, I’ll think I have them lined up properly, then I start doubting myself and have to go back over them. Even with the volunteers, I’ll think, “Did I already call her, or did I only write her name down to call?” and then I’m sorting through notes trying to reconstruct it.

So yes, I do have trouble keeping track, but it’s mostly that I keep mixing up these simple, ordinary things even after I’ve looked at them. It makes me feel like I can’t quite rely on my own head.
Does the confusion you're experiencing tend to come and go, or does it feel like it's been consistently present throughout the day, every day?

It feels pretty consistent, honestly. I wouldn’t say it’s like a wave that comes over me for a minute and then I’m completely clear again. It’s more that throughout the day my head just feels… foggy, like I have to work harder to keep ordinary things straight.

That’s really what brought me in. I keep mixing up simple things—appointment times, exhibit dates, and even which volunteer I already called versus who I only meant to call. I’ll think I’ve got it sorted out, and then a little later I’m unsure again and have to go back and check. So it’s not one dramatic spell of confusion so much as this ongoing muddled feeling that seems to be there most of the day, every day lately.
Do you ever find it hard to remember the order in which events happened, like whether something occurred this morning, yesterday, or last week, even after thinking about it carefully?

Yes… yes, that’s part of what I mean, I think. I can usually eventually piece it together if I sit there and really think it through, but it doesn’t come easily. My head feels foggy, and I keep mixing up these simple things that I feel like I should just know.

Like with appointments, I’ll have the time in my mind, and then suddenly I’m not sure if that was the one I wrote down or just the one I thought it was. Or the exhibit dates—I’ll try to remember what comes first and what happened when, and I’ll get turned around. And with the volunteers, I’ll think, “Did I already call her, or was that someone I meant to call?” Then I go back over it again and again.

So it’s not always that I completely forget everything, but the order of things gets muddled, and even after thinking carefully, I don’t feel very confident. That fogginess is really what scared me enough to come in.

Do you ever have trouble recognizing common objects or remembering the names of familiar items, like forgetting what a spoon is used for or not being able to recall the word for something you see every day?

I don’t think so… not in that way, at least. If I’m looking at a spoon, I know it’s a spoon, and I know what I’d use it for. I haven’t been standing in the kitchen unable to recognize things or anything like that.

Sometimes a word might sit on the tip of my tongue for a moment, but I think that’s happened to me for years, and I don’t know that it’s the same as what you mean. The thing that worries me is more when I’m trying to keep information straight, not so much that I don’t know what everyday objects are called or what they’re for. So, no, I haven’t really noticed that particular problem.
Do you ever find it hard to navigate around places you know well, like getting lost in your own neighborhood or having trouble finding your way home?

No… I don’t think I’ve had that happen, not like getting lost coming home or not recognizing where I am. I mean, I still know my way around the places I’m used to. If I’m in my neighborhood or going somewhere familiar, I haven’t suddenly found myself unable to figure out where to turn.

Now, I may second-guess myself more than I used to—like, “Did I mean to go this way or that way?”—but I don’t think I’ve actually been lost. It’s more that I’ll pause and feel unsure for a moment, and then once I look around or think it through, I know where I am. I haven’t had to call anyone to come get me or anything like that.

So I’d say no, not really. That isn’t the part that’s been bothering me most.
Do you ever find it hard to remember recent conversations or events, like not being able to recall something that happened just a day or two ago, even after thinking about it?

Yes, that’s the kind of thing that’s been bothering me, though it’s not always that the whole conversation disappears. It’s more like my head feels foggy, and I can’t keep the pieces lined up the way I used to.

For example, with appointments, I’ll think I know the time, and then later I’m not sure if that was the actual time or just the time I had in my head. Or with the exhibit dates, I’ll get mixed up about what came first or which date goes with what. And with the volunteers, I’ll sit there thinking, “Did I already call her, or was she the one I was supposed to call next?” It sounds so simple when I say it out loud, but in the moment it feels very unsettling.

So yes, recent things can get muddled, especially if there are a few details involved. I can sometimes piece it back together if I really concentrate, but it doesn’t feel clear, and I don’t trust my memory the way I used to. That foggy feeling and mixing up simple things is really what brought me in.
Do you ever feel lost or disoriented in places you’ve been to many times, like your own home or a store you visit regularly?

No, I don’t think so—not in places like my own home or a regular store. I know where I am in the house, and I’m not wandering into a room and feeling like I don’t recognize it or anything like that.

At the grocery store, I might take longer to find something, but I think that’s more because stores move things around or I get distracted looking for one item and then remember another. I don’t feel lost, exactly. I still know how to get to the front, where the checkout is, where the parking lot is, that sort of thing.

So… no, I haven’t really felt disoriented in familiar places. It’s more that I may feel a little unsure or slowed down sometimes, but not like I don’t know where I am.
